items.title: Protein and biological data generation concepts
items.text: Protein and biological data generation concepts addresses how information is prepared, described, versioned, or governed. Validate the input, keep source and access metadata, handle duplicates and missing values deliberately, and test the downstream effect of a data change rather than treating the data pipeline as invisible plumbing.

items.title: Synthetic data for scientific workflows
items.text: Synthetic data for scientific workflows describes one part of a controlled action loop. The model may propose a step, but the application should independently validate the arguments, check the caller's permissions, enforce step/time limits, and record the actual tool result before deciding what happens next.

items.title: Domain-specific evaluation
items.text: Use domain-specific evaluation to turn a vague quality claim into an observable criterion. Define a representative dataset, an expected outcome or rubric, a baseline, and the failure categories you will record; interpret aggregate scores alongside examples and affected groups.

items.title: Scientific reproducibility and expert validation
items.text: Scientific reproducibility and expert validation supports a repeatable development workflow. Keep dependencies and model choices explicit, preserve small input/output fixtures, isolate credentials from source code, and document how another learner can reproduce the result on a compatible environment.

content_blocks.text: Model names, API payloads, supported modalities, quotas, pricing, and SDK behavior vary by provider and change over time. Treat linked official documentation as the authority for a live integration; examples here avoid hard-coded production model IDs and secrets.

content.task: Practice scientific literature analysis within scientific and domain-specific generative ai: use a small synthetic input, predict the result, run the example, then change one input to test an edge case. Record the expected result and one limitation.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example uses a clearly described, non-sensitive input.
Expected behavior and at least one edge/failure case are written down.
The learner checks the result against an explicit criterion and records limitations.
hints: Begin with a tiny input whose expected behavior you can explain before running it.
Change one variable at a time and retain a fixed baseline for comparison.
When a model or external service is involved, inspect evidence and errors; do not treat the model response as a trusted instruction.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming fluent or plausible output is necessarily correct.
common_mistakes.fix: Use evidence, schema checks, representative test cases, and human review for consequential results.

common_mistakes.mistake: Changing several inputs or parameters at once.
common_mistakes.fix: Keep a baseline and vary one factor at a time so the effect can be interpreted.

common_mistakes.mistake: Putting secrets or private source material in prompts, logs, or a public example.
common_mistakes.fix: Use synthetic data, server-side secret storage, data minimization, and reviewed retention rules.
